en: Related to the context window of models,
there is another important concept called
context rot.
The idea here behind this term or problem
is that in that context, in that
conversation, for example, that builds up
with a large language model, there may be
details
that don't really matter anymore. For
example, thoughts that were dismissed,
answers that turned out to be wrong.
Or anything like that. Maybe also
a PDF document you added which turned out to
be irrelevant.
All that information that may be in the
context window that's being sent to the
model with every turn that's no longer
relevant or that maybe never was relevant is
of course a problem because it's still all
context that will be considered by the model
for producing its answer and it may nudge
the model in the wrong direction. It may
lead to suboptimal output and it will
definitely also take up space in the context
window, which of course is limited,
which is unnecessarily taken up. Now,
besides irrelevant information in the
context window, context rot also simply
comes up if you
produce very long context windows, very
large context windows. Even if you are still
below the upper limit a model supports,
it is proven, it has been proven in studies
that the longer your context gets, the more
information you send send to the model,
the less precise and bad its responses tend
to get.
The danger of hallucinations is higher if
you are closer to the upper limit of the
context window. Which, by the way, besides a
cost factor, is also why that upper window
exists. It simply turned out that these
large language models produce vastly worse
results if the context is large.
And therefore, it's a good practice to
consider starting new sessions as your
context fills up, to maybe manually trigger
compaction from time to time if your tool
supports that, and to always consider which
information does matter to a model and which
information doesn't. Because thinking that
more is better is definitely a bad idea. You
don't want to feed a model everything that
could potentially matter. Instead, you want
to focus on sharing the information, the
sources, the details,
you know, that will matter. Because more
isn't better. Instead, more context leads to
worse results. Especially, of course, if
that context includes a lot of irrelevant
information.
